sources.title: The National Archives: Colonial administration records, Sierra Leone
sources.note: Sierra Leone country section: colony in 1808, hinterland protectorate in 1896. Administrative distinctions are essential for the early map.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Sierra Leone
sources.note: Recognition section dates independence to 27 April 1961, despite the atlas record beginning in 1960.

sources.title: World Monuments Fund: World Monuments Watch 2021, Bunce Island
sources.note: Printed page 45: building remains, rice-growing knowledge and the forced Atlantic movement of people.

sources.title: Sierra Leone Heritage: Old Fourah Bay College building
sources.note: Historical description from Freetown university and museum heritage survey: foundation in 1845, opening in 1848 and roof timbers from condemned slave ships.

sources.title: University of Sierra Leone: Fourah Bay College
sources.note: Institutional history gives foundation on 18 February 1827. Avoids its overbroad first-university claim.

sources.title: Sierra Leone Heritage: Country Cloth, BMAG:WA506709
sources.note: Museum catalogue, production before 1899; Mende attribution, sixteen blue strips and strip-weaving technique. Direct fetch failed; full indexed catalogue text was read.

sources.title: Malcolm Awadajin Finney: Krio, APiCS survey chapter
sources.note: 2013 linguistic survey; section 6.5, example 27, gives the exact written sample and translation. Sections 1 to 2 discuss Krio history and changing educational use.

sources.title: United Nations: UNAMSIL, The Story Behind the Success
sources.note: 2003 retrospective: disarmament, January 2002 end of war, May elections, rebuilding civil authority and reintegration.

sources.title: UNICEF: Supporting girls in Sierra Leone to ensure safe and dignified menstrual hygiene management
sources.note: Harriet Mason, 28 February 2023; Services Secondary School, peer mentors, reusable kits and boys participation.

sources.title: UNICEF: Engaging boys in menstrual hygiene management
sources.note: Tapuwa Mutseyekwa, 14 March 2022; named example of Abdul and Daniella Sesay in Jui.

sources.title: The National Archives: Colonial administration records, Gambia
sources.note: Gambia country section: Bathurst colony, inland protectorate administration from 1894, 1965 independence and 1970 republic.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: The Gambia
sources.note: Independence on 18 February 1965; Bathurst later named Banjul.

sources.title: UNESCO: Kunta Kinteh Island and Related Sites
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value: distinct functions of island fort, warehouses, Six-Gun Battery of 1816 and Fort Bullen of 1826. Earlier Phoenician and first-trade-route claims are not used.

sources.title: UNESCO: Kankurang, Manding initiatory rite
sources.note: Public heritage description, inscribed 2008; bark and fibre costume, teaching and forest pressures. No secret ritual knowledge is inferred.

sources.title: Boston University: Conversation with Ousman Kijera 2
sources.note: 2022 educational resource; metadata gives Banjul birth and study in The Gambia/Casamance. Glossary item 43 supplies exact Latin-script Mandinka expression and translation.

sources.title: LSHTM: Vaccination to reduce the global burden of invasive pneumococcal disease
sources.note: Research institution account: 2000 to 2004 randomized trial, mortality reduction; 2009 introduction and subsequent surveillance.

sources.title: UNICEF: When Water Came to Sambel Dakka
sources.note: Momodou Muctarr Jallow, 11 May 2026. Solar-powered supply, former bicycle water journeys, ventilated pit latrines, resident testimony.

sources.title: United Nations Security Council: Resolution 2337 and the Gambian transition
sources.note: 19 January 2017 meeting report and resolution text; December 2016 election and demand for transfer of power.

sources.title: US Department of State: Background Notes, Eritrea, March 1998
sources.note: Historical section: 1962 annexation, referendum, April recognition and May 1993 formal celebration. Indexed historical text read; direct archive returns technical difficulties. Its implication that armed resistance began only in 1962 is not adopted.

sources.title: United Nations Yearbook 1952: Political and Security Questions
sources.note: Eritrea section records the federation under the Ethiopian Crown becoming effective in September 1952.

sources.title: The National Archives: Other countries and territories
sources.note: Eritrea table: Italian colony 1890 to 1941; Ethiopian annexation from 1962. Other country entries are not relied on.

sources.title: UNESCO: Asmara, a Modernist African City
sources.note: Description and Outstanding Universal Value: planning 1893 to 1941, racial zoning, indigenous quarters, local skills and public architecture.

sources.title: Asmara: Africa’s Secret Modernist City, exhibition catalogue
sources.note: Exhibition catalogue hosted by the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano. Human PDF page 16: Giuseppe Pettazzi, Fiat Tagliero, 1938, 30-metre freestanding concrete roof. Human PDF page 15: Enda Mariam, 1938/39 and local building forms.

sources.title: Haddas Ertra, 24 December 2025
sources.note: Primary newspaper issue, printed masthead on page 1: ሓዳስ ኤርትራ. A specimen of state newspaper typography, not independent evidence for political claims.

sources.title: Index on Censorship: A press in the making
sources.note: Contemporary 1993 report identifies Hadas Eritra as New Eritrea and describes its first issue on 1 September 1991. Used only for title translation and historical publication context.

sources.title: UNICEF / UN Eritrea: A girl in her periods faces so much discomfort at school
sources.note: 11 July 2022: Adi-Baro school, Sesen Mihtreteab, separate latrines, medical room, reservoir water and games.

sources.title: WHO Results Report: Eritrea, 2024 country profile
sources.note: 2024 results section on measles investigation, no reported outbreaks/deaths, and laboratory testing of 58 acute flaccid paralysis cases with no wild poliovirus detected. Not a claim of certified measles eradication.

sources.title: United Nations Eritrea: Annual Results Report 2025
sources.note: Education story: Kerkebet Boarding School, opened 2022, Bedawit communities, solar ICT classrooms and distant villages.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch: World Report 2025, Eritrea
sources.note: Dated rights-monitoring report describing indefinite national service, lack of elections and unimplemented 1997 constitution. Attributed explicitly; not used as a timeless statement about every individual.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Mauritania
sources.note: Recognition section: independence from French sovereignty on 28 November 1960.

sources.title: UNESCO: Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata
sources.note: Description and Outstanding Universal Value: caravan towns, courtyard houses, stone decoration, warehouses and desert conservation pressures. Earlier heritage is distinct from the modern republic.

sources.title: UNESCO: Mahadra, a community system for transmission of traditional knowledge and oral expressions
sources.note: 2023 inscription: tent classrooms, oral memorization, environmental knowledge, poetry and community teaching.

sources.title: Mauritanian Constitutional Council: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania
sources.note: Official Arabic consolidated text of the 20 July 1991 constitution, including 2017 revisions. Article 9 exact motto; article 6 and preamble list national languages.

sources.title: Mauritanian Constitutional Council: Response on fraternity
sources.note: Council document, constitutional motto in French: Honneur, Fraternité, Justice. Supports English translation of the Arabic sample.

sources.title: Banc d’Arguin National Park: Local development, the Imraguen
sources.note: Park authority description of fishing on foot and from lateen-sailed lanches; motorboats prohibited.

sources.title: Banc d’Arguin National Park: Management Plan 2010 to 2014
sources.note: Printed page 57 reviews fish processing, women’s poutargue marketing and village cooperatives. A dated management record, not a current census.

sources.title: UNICEF: A brighter life for every child with sustainable energy
sources.note: Printed page 19, Mauritania case study: boreholes, solar pumping, operator training in 2020 and 2021; photograph caption on women’s market garden.

sources.title: UN Peacebuilding Commission: Mauritania meeting concept note, 20 March 2024
sources.note: Background describes the 2019 first democratic transfer between elected presidents.

sources.title: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child: Mauritania concluding observations, 2018
sources.note: Paragraph 24: criminal-law changes in 2015 and continuing reports of caste-based slavery affecting children; recommendations on education, family reunification and justice.

sources.title: United Nations Juridical Yearbook 1974
sources.note: Printed page 170, paragraph 20 (PDF page 186): proclamation on 24 September 1973 and change in international status.

sources.title: Portuguese Republic: Declaration recognizing Guinea-Bissau independence
sources.note: Declaration signed 10 September 1974, published 11 September; exact recognition text.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Guinea-Bissau
sources.note: Recognition and embassy sections: former Portuguese territory; US recognition in 1974 and suspension of embassy operations during civil war in June 1998.

sources.title: Tiago Saraiva: Black Science, Amílcar Cabral’s Agricultural Survey and the Seeds of African Decolonization
sources.note: Isis 113(3), 2022, pages 597 to 609. Figure 2 and Sampling and Development section: survey methods, Maria Helena Rodrigues and household research.

sources.title: Casa Comum: PAIGC reading-book circular, December 1964
sources.note: Fundação Mário Soares e Maria Barroso, Amílcar Cabral archive, item 07073.132.014. Indexed catalogue directly verifies date and announced book title; direct viewer fetch failed.

sources.title: Intumbo, Inverno and Holm: Guinea-Bissau Kriyol
sources.note: APiCS survey 33, 2013: sociolinguistic section and example 9, exact written sentence and translation.

sources.title: UNESCO: Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago, Omatí Minhô
sources.note: 2025 inscription; criteria, species, traditional management and marine protected areas.

sources.title: UNICEF: Ending open defecation in Guinea-Bissau, it all starts under a mango tree
sources.note: 3 July 2019: Quinara’s 2018 certification, community meetings, locally built toilets and follow-up visits.

sources.title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau: Water, sanitation and hygiene
sources.note: Resources section explicitly dates mWATER mapping to 2016 and 2018; distinguishes functioning water points from mere infrastructure counts.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Djibouti
sources.note: Recognition and relations sections: French sovereignty, independence and embassy conversion on 27 June 1977.

sources.title: Raphaël Cotteverte: Le territoire français des Afars et des Issas
sources.note: Revue historique des Armées 27(3), 1971, pages 4 to 6: 1967 name change, territorial institutions and towns. Used as contemporary colonial administrative evidence, not endorsement of its celebratory political assessment.

sources.title: Presidency of Djibouti: Constitution
sources.note: Article 1 exact French motto and official languages. English translation of the three motto words supplied editorially.

sources.title: UNESCO: Djibouti considers nominating Abourma Rock Art site
sources.note: 2019 expert mission account: prehistoric rock engravings, Tadjoura region and conservation. A proposed site, not a World Heritage inscription.

sources.title: UNESCO: Xeer Ciise, oral customary laws of Somali-Issa communities
sources.note: 2024 inscription, shared by Ethiopia, Djibouti and Somalia: reconciliation, compensation and transmission through stories, poetry and education. Indexed official text read; direct fetch gives minimal page.

sources.title: UNESCO: Xeedho
sources.note: 2023 urgent safeguarding inscription: food, carved container, decorations and women’s family knowledge.

sources.title: UNESCO Committee decision 16.COM 8.a.5
sources.note: 2021 nomination discussion specifies Somali community and groom/friends untying hidden knots; not the later inscription decision.

sources.title: UNICEF: Improved drinking water saving lives in Beyadeh
sources.note: 30 April 2019, report from 6 March: solar water system, family testimony and school sanitation.

sources.title: Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority: Rail
sources.note: Commercial operations started January 2018; railway links container and cargo terminals with Ethiopia. Omit internally inconsistent investment total.

sources.title: Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority: French auditors visit ship repair and port infrastructures
sources.note: 1 March 2026 dated operator account: ship-repair facility dimensions, functions and 20,000-ton lifting capacity. Omit erroneous claim that old railway was Africa’s first.

sources.title: WHO results report: Djibouti, 2024 country profile
sources.note: Malaria response section: therapeutic efficacy study, treatment-policy update and insecticide resistance.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Equatorial Guinea
sources.note: Recognition section: independence from Spain on 12 October 1968; embassy history identifies Santa Isabel as later Malabo.

sources.title: Enrique Martino: Clandestine Recruitment Networks in the Bight of Biafra
sources.note: International Review of Social History 57, 2012, pages 39 to 72; opening pages describe coercive recruitment from Rio Muni and Nigeria to cocoa plantations on Fernando Po.

sources.title: Alejandro Artucio: The Trial of Macias in Equatorial Guinea
sources.note: International Commission of Jurists observer report, 1979. Printed pages 5, 20 and preface: repression, 3 August coup, and limitations of the subsequent trial.

sources.title: World Bank: Equatorial Guinea Country Economic Memorandum 2025
sources.note: 4 March 2025 research summary: oil boom in 1990s, declining revenues and need to invest in education and health.

sources.title: Kofi Yakpo: Pichi
sources.note: 2013 APiCS survey 19; 2003 to 2007 fieldwork, historical contact with Krio and role of Spanish.

sources.title: Kofi Yakpo: Pichi polar questions
sources.note: APiCS example 19-197, source Yakpo 2009 page 118: exact Pichi question and English translation. Indexed official entry read; direct fetch failed.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Eyema byeri, reliquary guardian figure
sources.note: Object 1978.412.441, nineteenth century, Okak-Fang artist, Gabon or Equatorial Guinea. Location uncertainty is retained in prose.

sources.title: Bioko Marine Turtle Program: Research
sources.note: Research team account: 2018 satellite tagging of six green turtles, 2019 completed project; local field assistants and conservation camps.

sources.title: WHO Bulletin: Testing indoor residual spraying coverage targets for malaria control, Bioko
sources.note: 2025 original research abstract: 2021 and 2022 comparison of 50% and 80% household coverage, annual rapid diagnostic testing. Indexed WHO full abstract read; direct PDF fetch failed. No universal treatment recommendation inferred.

sources.title: UNICEF: Equatorial Guinea country programme document, 2023
sources.note: Paragraphs 11 and 14, printed pages 4 and 5: preliminary 2023 handwashing data and COVID school-closure distance education.

sources.title: UNICEF: Launch of the National School Health Programme in Equatorial Guinea
sources.note: 20 October 2025 press release about launch in Bata on 18 October; distinguishes plans and early pilot from achieved national coverage.

sources.title: UNESCO: Island of Saint-Louis
sources.note: Brief synthesis and authenticity: 1659 trading settlement, 1897 bridge, French West African capital until 1902.

sources.title: Alain Sinou: Saint-Louis du Sénégal au début du XIXe siècle, du comptoir à la ville
sources.note: Cahiers d’études africaines 29, 1989, pages 377 to 395. Introduction and indexed printed page 378: local merchants, dependence on mainland supplies and political/urban change.

sources.title: George E. Brooks: Artists’ depiction of Senegalese signares
sources.note: Academic bibliography’s indexed abstract of nineteenth-century representations: property, houses and domestic enslavement. Source used only for the explicitly summarized findings.

sources.title: City of Saint-Louis: Découverte
sources.note: Municipal heritage description of surviving houses: ground-floor shops, high ceilings, balconies and verandas. No romanticized signare commentary adopted.

sources.title: Roger Pasquier: Un aspect de l’histoire des villes du Sénégal, les problèmes de ravitaillement au XIXe siècle
sources.note: 1987 research, Les cahiers de la recherche agronomique 5, pages 177 to 213. Indexed scholarly abstract summarizes 1840 to 1870 millet, wheat and rice supply; direct page fetch failed.

sources.title: Jean-Baptiste and Roberts: Runaway Enslaved Families in Senegal, 1857 to 1903
sources.note: 2025 original research abstract: nearly 29,000 liberation claims; study identifies 1,445 individuals in family units, 90% of units headed by women.

sources.title: P.-David Boilat: Grammaire de la langue woloffe, 1858
sources.note: Digitized original book metadata and contents: exact French title, author, Imprimerie Impériale and 1858 publication. Translation supplied editorially; no unverified Wolof transcription copied.

sources.title: Boston University African Studies Center: African Ajami
sources.note: Research programme description: African languages written in adapted Arabic scripts, Wolof manuscript preservation and scholarly language training.

sources.title: John Cropper: Running on Empty, Fossil Fuels, Local Fuels and Entangled Infrastructures in Colonial Senegal
sources.note: Journal of African History 63, 2022, pages 19 to 36. Railway completed 1885; household and migrant labour, peanut byproducts and local fuels.

sources.title: UNESCO: William Ponty School Collection of Papers
sources.note: Teacher-training college created by order of 24 November 1903; student papers from 1933 are later legacy, explicitly distinguished.

sources.title: French National Assembly: Blaise Diagne biography
sources.note: 1914 campaign for lycée, teacher-training and medical schools, conscience rights; election on 10 May 1914.

sources.title: Tobias Warner: Enduring Epidemic, Aesthetic Aftershocks of the 1914 Plague and the Segregation of Dakar
sources.note: 2022 original research abstract, eviction and house burning, general strike and creation of Médina.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: Senegal
sources.note: 1960 independence from France and later withdrawal from Mali Federation; supports distinction from imported 1878 and 1914 endpoints.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared, explicitly phased territorial history, not synonymous political status. Earlier atlas coverage 1815 to 1938; later begins 1960, independence is 1961. Coast colony 1808 and inland protectorate 1896 distinguished publicly. Decoded geometry in identities.json; early coastal polygons are generalized, not proof of inland control.

Shared phased narrative. Imported 1878 to 1914 and 1914 onward river-corridor polygons are consecutive colonial/modern coverage, not two independent polities; independence 1965, republic 1970. Earlier footprint is shorter upriver. No assertion of sovereign Gambia in 1878 or 1914.

Shared territorial history with explicit political phases, not identical sovereign states. Imported early coverage 1920 to 1938 is Italian colonial; 1960 coverage is Ethiopian federation, followed by annexation in 1962 and independence in 1993. Same general geography supports shared chronology, not independence at either map start. British administration between Italian defeat and federation is not assigned an invented map date.

Modern republic only, imported 1960 onward. Not ancient mauretania. Decoded first and modern polygons match general contemporary geography. No border outline used to adjudicate Western Sahara sovereignty; medieval heritage explicitly background rather than republic foundation.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: 1920 to present imported record covers Portuguese Guinea and the later republic. Proclamation 24 September 1973 and Portuguese recognition 10 September 1974 are distinguished; no independence assigned to 1920.
1945 to present outline spans French colonial administration, 1967 territorial renaming and independent republic from 27 June 1977. It is not an independent state from 1945.

1914 to present imported record spans colony and independent republic. Early decoded geometry includes Bioko and Río Muni but omits Annobón; public warning included. Nineteenth-century Fang object has uncertain Gabon/Equatorial Guinea provenance, stated explicitly.

Shared regional narrative, explicitly NOT an assertion of unchanged polity identity. Early 1530 to 1650 geometry extends south to latitude 9.274 and is incompatible with modern Senegal or a French colony founded in 1530. Later early-record geometry is coastal Senegal; 1900 to 1914 record is a larger colonial footprint. Narrative explicitly phases these labels and leaves existing senegal-1960 card untouched.
